item.message: Skill descriptions were shortened to fit the 2% skills context budget. Codex can still see every skill, but some descriptions are shorter. Disable unused skills or plugins to leave more room for the rest.

Neither verified boundary yet establishes whether new resources belong to a person, a collaborative project, or the entire deployment.","impact":"This determines authorization keys, database ownership fields, sharing commands, tab filtering, conflict handling, and whether future collaboration can grow without exposing one operator's private work to every user.","question":"What should be the default ownership boundary for newly created NexusCentral resources?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Private creation, explicit project sharing","consequence":"Conversations and drafts begin under one user, then selected workflows and related runs can be shared into a collaborative project. This adds explicit sharing transitions now but provides strong isolation and flexible collaboration long term."},{"number":2,"text":"Project-owned by default","consequence":"Every resource is created inside a selected collaborative project and is immediately visible to its members. This simplifies team collaboration but adds project-selection friction to individual work."},{"number":3,"text":"Deployment-wide shared","consequence":"All users see and operate on the same resources immediately. It can include the run record, queued job, initial state event, and idempotency key used—", "evidence":"`services/nexus-node/src/run-coordinator.mjs` accepts `runs.submit`, while `kits/jobs-kit/index.mjs` owns durable jobs and leases and `adapters/runtime-adapters/src/sqlite-store.mjs` persists state in SQLite WAL. The verified architecture does not specify whether these records commit together or are repaired after a partial crash.","impact":"This sets the core reliability contract for every Work and Workflow submission, determines recovery complexity, and decides whether a successful API response always identifies work that can resume after an immediate host crash.","question":"What durability guarantee must NexusCentral provide before returning success from a work-submission command?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Commit run and job atomically","consequence":"The canonical run, queued job, idempotency key, and initial event commit in one transaction before success. This requires a strict shared persistence boundary now but prevents accepted work from becoming orphaned long term."},{"number":2,"text":"Commit run, then repair queue","consequence":"The run becomes durable first and recovery recreates a missing job after a crash. This reduces transaction coupling but requires a permanent reconciliation subsystem and permits temporarily unexecutable accepted runs."},{"number":3,"text":"Commit job, then create run","consequence":"The queue accepts work first and the coordinator later materializes its run record. This favors queue throughput but allows jobs without visible canonical runs and complicates Runs-tab authority."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"Atomic acceptance best satisfies the locked crash-safe authority model and gives clients an unambiguous promise: success means both the authoritative record and executable work survived.","priority":96},{"decision_key":"client_event_replay_contract","label":"Resumable client events","context":"A replay cursor is a saved sequence position that lets a reconnecting client request events it missed. For example, a Runs tab reopening after a network interruption could resume after event 42 instead of trusting only a", "evidence":"`packages/central-client/index.mjs` serves HTTP/WebSocket clients, and `packages/contracts/index.mjs` defines canonical run transitions such as running, approval_required, and completed. The verified architecture does not define ordering, replay, or reconnect behavior for those transitions.","impact":"This changes the public event contract, stored event metadata, reconnect UX, integration reliability, and whether multiple clients can render the same authoritative history without polling races.","question":"What event-delivery contract should HTTP/WebSocket clients receive for conversations, workflows, runs, approvals, and provider health?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Ordered replay per resource","consequence":"Each conversation, workflow, run, or provider stream has monotonic sequence numbers and a replay cursor, with snapshots used for reconciliation. This adds sequence and retention rules now but gives reliable reconnects without imposing costly global ordering."},{"number":2,"text":"One host-wide ordered log","consequence":"Every event shares one deployment sequence and cursor. This simplifies whole-system audit replay but couples unrelated domains, increases retention pressure, and may become a scaling bottleneck."},{"number":3,"text":"Snapshots plus best-effort events","consequence":"Clients fetch current state and receive live events only while connected. This is simplest initially but missed transitions require polling and external integrations cannot reliably reconstruct history."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"Per-resource ordered replay preserves authoritative history and robust reconnects while keeping unrelated domains independently scalable.","priority":91}]}
